newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Rao arrives at court to face forgery case.
newsitem.headline: India's Rao arrives at court to face forgery case.

text.p: Former Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao arrived at a heavily-guarded makeshift court on Wednesday to face criminal forgery charges.
Paramilitary commandos ushered Rao, 75, from a bullet-proof car to an annexe at New Delhi's Vigyan Bhavan conference hall complex for his first appearance in the 1989 case.

Rao is the first former or serving prime minister to appear in court to face criminal charges. Former prime minister Indira Gandhi was summoned to court in a civil case in 1977 after a state of emergency imposed by her ended.

In the courtroom, Rao was flanked by two plainclothes paramilitary commandos and given a front seat away from three other people accused in the case, including a former minister and a religious Hindu guru close to the ex-prime minister.
Rao sat expressionless in a court that had allowed a few reporters and members of his Congress party to be present.
He had been scheduled to appear in court in September.

But two cases -- one involving alleged forgery, the other criminal conspiracy to cheat -- became bogged down in procedural manoeuvres, and Rao has been spared the humiliation of either a court appearance or being taken into custody.

The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), India's federal police, on September 26 charged Rao and the three others with involvement in an alleged attempt in 1989 to defame V.P. Singh, a Congress party rebel who later became prime minister.
They are alleged to have forged documents which aimed to show that Singh's son held $21 million in a bank account on the Caribbean island of St Kitts.
Rao has not commented publicly on the case.
Some 300 police ringed the spacious international conference centre, where a special court room has been set up to handle two trials involving Rao, senior security official Aditya Arya said.
Rao, who launched economic reforms but was hobbled by corruption charges, served from mid-1991 to last May when his Congress party was defeated in general elections.

He has been named but not formally charged in the 1983 cheating case. A hearing in the case is set for November 6 in the same court room. Both the forgery and cheating cases carry maximum penalties of seven years in jail.
The cavernous Vigyan Bhavan centre was chosen by police as a replacement site for crowded local courts where they feared an attack on the former prime minister.
Rao stepped down as Congress leader in September after a local judge upheld a summons ordering him to appear in court in the criminal cheating case.
But Rao, who said he was innocent of the charge of cheating a businessman out of $100,000 in 1983, has remained leader of Congress's parliamentary delegation and retains political clout.
His influence is magnified by Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's dependence on Congress support to help thwart potential challenges from right-wing Hindu nationalists in parliament.
Deve Gowda's 13-party centre-left coalition does not control an outright majority in the lower house of parliament and needs Congress's backing.

Rao's lawyer R.K. Anand, said that at Wednesday's hearing, his team would press chief metropolitan magistrate Prem Kumar to extend the temporary bail that has protected Rao from arrest but which expires on November 6.
